data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of truth, but as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in the logic of falsification: we prefer the theory that has survived severe tests because it has higher empirical content and has not yet been falsified, making it the best available target for future criticism. This preference does not smuggle in induction because it makes no claim about the future probability of the theory being true; it only asserts that, relative to our current critical discussion, this theory is the most worthy of further testing. The cost of accepting this view is the abandonment of the hope that science converges toward probable truth or even definable verisimilitude (given the Miller-Tichý refutation), leaving us with a purely procedural rationality where 'progress' is defined solely by the elimination of error, not the accumulation of confirmed knowledge.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If one can demonstrate that acting on the best-corroborated theory logically entails an assumption that the future will resemble the past (induction), then the preference is indefensible on Popperian terms.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the Miller-Tichý refutation implies that we cannot even rationally claim a falsified theory is 'further from the truth' than a surviving one, then the basis for preferring the survivor collapses into arbitrary convention.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If Popper's own practical advice to scientists relies on tacit inductive assumptions despite his explicit denials, then his system is internally inconsistent.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between the logical status of a theory (which cannot be probabilified) and the methodological decision of which theory to subject to further tests. It leverages the concept of 'empirical content' (boldness) to explain why surviving severe tests matters: a bold theory that survives is more informative than a cautious one, regardless of its truth probability. It addresses the Miller-Tichý refutation by conceding that verisimilitude cannot be formally defined as a guide, forcing the defense to rest entirely on the negative achievement of error elimination rather than positive approximation to truth.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": ["Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of truth, but as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in the logic of falsific"]}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
